primary.thesis: The rules say the by-election follows Farage's announced resignation from Clacton. A sitting MP who resigns his seat usually does so to leave the Commons or to move on to another role or seat, not to stand again in the seat he just gave up. If Farage is not on the ballot, the rules send the market to the lowest bracket, so '<40%' is the default outcome. It also covers the case where the result is not certified by the June 2027 deadline. A second path is that Farage resigns to seek a fresh mandate and stands again. If so, his 2024 general-election share of about 46% in a multi-party field suggests a result in the 40s, not a landslide, especially if the main parties campaign hard against him or the seat sees tactical voting. So the basket takes the not-standing or timing route and the modest-recontest route, and leaves out the high brackets.

basket.reason: This bracket wins if Farage does not stand, if results are not definitive by 30 June 2027, or if he stands and underperforms. After a resignation, not standing is the most natural reading.
This covers a re-mandate by-election where he roughly repeats his 2024 share of about 46% against a field of Conservative, Labour and other candidates.
Winning 80% or more in a contested UK parliamentary by-election is almost unheard of, even for a dominant candidate, because the major parties normally field candidates.

failure_narrative: Farage's resignation is a deliberate move to stand again in Clacton as a show of strength or a personal referendum. Reform UK is polling at or near the top nationally, and the Conservatives, and perhaps Labour, stand down or run only token campaigns because they see a by-election they cannot win. Farage then takes more than 50% of a low-turnout vote, landing in the 50-60% or 60-70% bracket. That makes both C1 and C2 lose, and the only leg that pays is C6 NO.
hedge_thesis: The worlds where the basket fails are the ones where Reform UK and Farage are strong enough nationally to turn a by-election into a coronation. The hedge is a thesis about Westminster as a whole: Reform UK leads or nearly leads national voting-intention polls, is favoured to win the most seats at the next general election, and Farage is a leading contender to be the next prime minister. The mechanism has two parts. First, only a leader with strong national momentum would resign to recontest. Second, that same momentum, together with other parties declining to fight hard, is what pushes his local share above 50%. Instruments on Reform's national seat or vote share, or on Farage becoming prime minister, should pay in those same worlds.
